title: Messi Bathed Lamine Yamal as a Baby — 19 Years Later They Met in the World Cup Final | Did You Know?

card.title: The Bath Photo
card.subtitle: Did You Know? deep dive card
card.story: In 2007 a shy twenty-year-old Lionel Messi bathed a baby from Rocafonda for a charity calendar photo. The baby was Lamine Yamal. The pictures were forgotten for seventeen years, until the two met in the 2026 World Cup final.

beats.vo: July the nineteenth, twenty twenty-six. New Jersey. The World Cup final. Spain against Argentina.
On one side, Lionel Messi, chasing one last crown. On the other, Lamine Yamal, nineteen years old, the boy Spain has built its future around.
But did you know these two had met before? Nineteen years earlier. In a bathtub.
Chapter one. The raffle.
In two thousand and seven, Barcelona's club foundation teamed up with UNICEF and the newspaper Diario Sport to make a charity calendar.
The idea was simple. Families from the neighbourhoods around Barcelona would be photographed at the Camp Nou, with a first-team player.
In Rocafonda, a working-class district of Mataró, the families signed up for a raffle. One young couple won it.
His father was from Morocco. His mother, from Equatorial Guinea. Their son was a baby, born that July. His name was Lamine.
And the player chosen to hold him was a shy twenty-year-old from Rosario, in Argentina.
Lionel Messi.
Chapter two. The photo.
The photographer, Joan Monfort, set up a small plastic tub of water. Messi was asked to bathe the baby for the camera. He was shy, and careful, and he did it.
The pictures went into the calendar. The calendar raised its money. And then the photos simply disappeared. For seventeen years, almost nobody saw them.
In those years, Messi became the greatest player of his generation. His first Ballon d'Or in two thousand and nine. A World Cup in Qatar. Eight Ballon d'Or awards in all.
And the baby from Rocafonda grew up inside La Masia, Barcelona's academy. The same school that had made Messi.
In April twenty twenty-three, at fifteen years old, Lamine Yamal made his first-team debut for Barcelona.
Chapter three. The prophecy.
A few weeks earlier, against Croatia, he had already become the youngest player ever to appear at a European Championship. Sixteen years and three hundred and thirty-eight days old.
Summer, twenty twenty-four. The European Championship in Germany. Yamal is sixteen. In the semi-final against France, he cuts inside and curls a shot into the top corner from outside the box.
That night he also broke a record that had stood since nineteen fifty-eight, when Pelé was seventeen. Nobody younger had ever played in the semi-final of a major tournament.
He is the youngest player ever to score at a European Championship. Five days later, Spain are champions of Europe, and he is named the best young player of the tournament.
That summer, his father, Mounir Nasraoui, found the old photos and posted one online. His caption: the beginning of two legends.
The world could hardly believe it. Messi had once bathed the boy who was now being called the next Messi.
And every time Yamal scores, he points back to where it began. Three, zero, four. The last digits of Rocafonda's postcode.
Chapter four. The final.
On the road to that final, against Saudi Arabia on the twenty-first of June, Yamal scored his first World Cup goal. Only Gavi had ever scored for Spain at a World Cup at a younger age.
Which brings us back to New Jersey. Nineteen years after the bath photo, the two of them walk out for the biggest match in football.
Emiliano Martínez saves from Yamal. Unai Simón denies Messi. Ninety minutes, and nobody scores.
Then, in the hundred and sixth minute, Ferran Torres taps in from close range. Spain win one-nil. They are champions of the world.
Messi takes the Silver Ball as the tournament's second-best player. And the baby he once held in a plastic tub is a world champion at nineteen.
A charity raffle in Rocafonda. A shy twenty-year-old, a tub of water and a baby. Nineteen years later, the same two names in the same World Cup final.
